summary: Finding the stone taken away, Mary Magdalene runs to Simon Peter and the disciple whom Jesus loved and tells them someone has taken the Lord from the tomb.
key_insight: Mary’s first thought was theft, not resurrection. The most devoted follower at the tomb did not imagine that Jesus had risen, and her report sent two apostles to look for a missing body, not a living Lord.
story: Mary Magdalene had come to the tomb and seen that the stone was taken away.
She ran and came to Simon Peter, and to the other disciple, the one whom Jesus loved.
“They have taken away the Lord out of the tomb,” she told them, “and we do not know where they have laid Him.”

fit.question: In Matthew, Mark and Luke the women hear from angels that Jesus is risen. Here Mary tells Peter only that the body has been taken. Did she not hear the angels?

points.label: She left at once
points.text: John says Mary saw the stone taken away and ran. The most natural reading is that she turned back as soon as she saw the open tomb, before the other women went in and met the angels. McGarvey and many others read it this way.

points.label: Her report fits what she knew
points.text: She says nothing of angels or of a risen Lord, only that the body is gone. That is what someone would say who had seen an open tomb and nothing more. When she returns, she says the same thing to the angels (John 20:13).

fit.note: Mary left before the angels spoke, and her report fits that order. The accounts fit together.
fit.short: Mary ran back as soon as she saw the open tomb, before the other women went in and heard the angels.

scene.label: The disciple whom Jesus loved
scene.text: John never names himself in his Gospel. He calls himself “the other disciple” or “the disciple whom Jesus loved” (John 21:20, 24), and from early times the church has identified him as John the son of Zebedee.

scene.label: Peter after his denial
scene.text: Early on Friday morning Peter had denied Jesus three times, and he “went out and wept bitterly” (Luke 22:62). Two days later Mary still ran to him. Peter and John are often found together (Luke 22:8; Acts 3:1).

scene.label: “They have taken”
scene.text: Mary does not say who. Tombs in the ancient world were sometimes robbed or disturbed, and a body could be moved by those in charge of a burial place. An empty tomb, on its own, suggested to her nothing more.

witnesses.john: Only John records Mary’s run to Peter and the beloved disciple. He tells how the news of the empty tomb first reached the apostles, as one of the two men who heard it, and he lets Mary’s honest confusion stand. In John, faith in the risen Jesus does not begin with expectation; it begins with an empty tomb no one could explain.

seeing.reveals: Mary still calls Him “the Lord” while she believes His body has been stolen. Jesus had won a devotion that His death did not end, and He was about to answer it Himself.
seeing.living: Mary told what she saw and admitted what she did not know. When grief or confusion comes, bring it honestly to the people of Jesus rather than carrying it alone. That morning, Mary’s confused report sent two disciples running toward the truth.
seeing.ponder: When Jesus seems absent, do you still speak of Him as “the Lord”?

preaching.big_idea: Mary’s love ran ahead of her understanding, and it sent others to the empty tomb.
outline: A report full of love and confusion (2b)
preaching.watch_for: Mary’s words about where He has been laid come three times in the chapter (vv. 2, 13, 15). Her search for a body ends only when Jesus speaks her name (v. 16).

title: Mary Magdalene Runs to Tell Peter
